title: Gene Regulation
text:
The SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex is an enzyme that slides and evicts nucleosomes to open chromatin for other factors, so that changes in gene expression follow changes in accessibility. We’re interested in finding how this complex transcription while accessibility stays the same. The complex therefore also acts as a scaffold, recruiting regulatory proteins independently of its remodeling activity. We study what controls that scaffolding and how the partners SWI/SNF recruits produce specific changes in gene expression.
Our current projects focus on two ways SWI/SNF partners are regulated. One is post-translational modification of SWI/SNF subunits. CARM1 methylates an arginine on the core subunit BAF155. This methylation does not change which version of the complex assembles, but it changes the proteins the complex contacts, particularly the RNA processing machinery, and can alter transcription without any change in chromatin accessibility. The other input is RNA itself. SWI/SNF and related remodelers bind RNA and act at several steps of the transcription cycle, including polymerase pausing, splicing, and 3′ end processing, and RNA can tune the complex’s interactions on a transcript-by-transcript basis.
Our goal is to define how SWI/SNF and related remodelers select their regulatory partners and how that selection shapes gene regulation beyond accessibility. We use chromatin profiling, gene expression analysis, and interaction proteomics to link specific modifications and RNA contacts to the genes they control.

title: Chromatin Disruption in Liver Cancer
text:
Liver cancer is the third leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) accounts for most cases. Its incidence continues to rise, driven by viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, and alcohol-related liver disease. Immune checkpoint inhibitors are now standard first-line therapy for advanced disease, but fewer than a third of patients respond and durable benefit is uncommon. Work on why has concentrated on the immune compartment. We study how the chromatin state of the tumor cell controls whether the immune system recognizes and kills it.
Chromatin regulators are among the most frequently mutated genes in HCC. The BAF form of the SWI/SNF remodeling complex alone is disrupted in about one in five liver tumors, a large genetic subset with no targeted therapy. We are studying the idea that altered BAF function in these tumor cells creates dependent chromatin states that can be targeted.
We are identifying the chromatin regulators that BAF-mutant liver tumors depend on to maintain these altered states, and testing whether removing them improve therapy responses. To keep the tumor and immune system together, we pair pooled, epigenome-focused CRISPR screens in immunocompetent orthotopic liver tumors with T-cell killing assays in BAF-mutant liver cancer lines. We want to find chromatin regulators whose loss reprograms immune-response pathways and to nominate combinations that could make immunotherapy work in a subtype of liver cancer that has few options.
